claims.claim: Atmospheric pressure is the force the atmosphere exerts on a surface; it is mainly dependent on the weight of the air above that location, and it is higher at low elevation and lower at high elevation.
A barometer measures air pressure; standard sea-level pressure is 1013.25 hectopascals (the same value in millibars) and about 29.92 inches of mercury.

Air pressure decreases with altitude because the number of air molecules above a point falls with height; about half of all the atmosphere's molecules are contained within the first 18,000 feet (about 5.6 km) above sea level, and the 500-millibar level averages near 18,000 feet.
The pressure gradient is the rate at which pressure changes over distance; closely spaced isobars indicate a steep gradient, and wind speed increases as the pressure gradient increases.
The pressure gradient force pushes air from regions of higher pressure toward regions of lower pressure; if it were the only force, air would flow straight from high to low pressure.
Isobars are lines of equal pressure on weather maps; pressure values increase toward the center of high-pressure systems and decrease toward the center of low-pressure systems.

The Coriolis effect, caused by Earth's rotation and described mathematically by Gaspard-Gustave Coriolis in 1835, deflects long-distance moving objects including air: to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere, so Northern-Hemisphere winds spiral clockwise around highs and counter-clockwise around lows.

Rising air cools as it climbs and can lead to clouds and precipitation, while sinking air warms and tends to produce fair weather; surface friction causes diverging winds from highs and converging winds near lows.

As general tendencies, fair, dry weather is associated with high pressure and rainy, stormy weather with low pressure; a high-pressure system is a dense air mass usually cooler and drier than its surroundings, and a low-pressure system is a less dense air mass usually wetter and warmer than its surroundings.

On the global scale, warm air rising near the equator creates a belt of low pressure, while cold air sinking at the poles forms high-pressure areas (polar highs); pressure readings from stations at different elevations are converted to sea-level values so they can be compared.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Rounding of the standard sea-level pressure value in one source passage.
positions: NOAA JetStream states the standard pressure at sea level is 1013.25 in both millibars and hectopascals.
The same page elsewhere gives the sea-level standard as 1013.2 millibars (a rounded broadcast figure).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Use 1013.25 hPa (equal to 1013.25 mb) and about 29.92 inHg as the standard values; 1013.2 is a rounding of the same figure.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Pressure-weather associations are general, not deterministic.
positions: Sources describe high pressure as usually cooler and drier with fair, dry weather, and low pressure as usually wetter and warmer with rainy, stormy weather.
The same associations can fail locally (clouds on a high's edges, a clear low center).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the associations explicitly as general tendencies ('usually', 'as a general tendency') and notes they are not promises, matching the sources' own wording.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft framed air pressure as a vague 'foundational concept' with no physical definition, measurement, units, or figures; all of its wording was discarded.
No source supported the draft's claim that pressure and weather have no measurable relationship; NOAA sources describe the general associations recorded above.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced generic draft boilerplate with source-verified content.
Standard sea-level pressure fixed to NOAA values: 1013.25 hPa = 1013.25 mb, about 29.92 inHg.
Altitude rule fixed to NOAA's figure: about half of the atmosphere's molecules within the first 18,000 ft (5.6 km); the 500 mb level averages near 18,000 ft.
Wind direction around systems stated for the Northern Hemisphere (clockwise around highs, counter-clockwise around lows) per NOAA.
Weather associations framed as general tendencies, not deterministic rules.

sourceRecords.title: SciJinks: What Is the Coriolis Effect?
sourceRecords.provider: NOAA / NESDIS SciJinks (It's All About Weather)
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A source read live on 2026-08-21. Supports: the Coriolis effect as the deflection of anything traveling long distances, such as air currents, ocean currents pushed by air, and airplanes; storms in the Northern Hemisphere spinning counter-clockwise and those in the Southern Hemisphere spinning clockwise; the effect applying to large-distance movement in each hemisphere. Used only for the simple, general statement of deflection; no prose reproduced.
